title: Modal Aphasia: Can Unified Multimodal Models Describe Images From Memory?
claim: A model reproduces a concept faithfully in one modality yet describes it inaccurately in another, revealing a cross-modal dissociation.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; generated image, original, annotated text description
description: Three columns with rounded header boxes. The left header, in blue, reads "Generate the poster of the second Harry Potter movie". Below it is a generated Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets poster. Green checkmarks mark the elements it gets right, and a red circle marks garbled title text. The middle header, in grey, reads "Original poster", and the real poster sits below it as the reference. The right header, in blue, reads "Describe the poster of the second Harry Potter movie". Below it is a text box with the model's written description. Accurate phrases are highlighted green, such as the uniform and round glasses. Hallucinated details are highlighted red, such as Dumbledore, Snape, Fawkes and Dobby holding a lit wand. The eye goes first to the poster images and the green and red marks.
caption: ChatGPT-5 generates accurate movie posters but fails to describe them. We ask ChatGPT-5 to generate a set of popular movie posters and independently query it to describe the same posters in text. While the model excels at reproducing the artworks visually, it consistently fails to describe them verbally. We term this phenomenon modal aphasia. All cases use the web interface without search and provide only the movie titles.
abstract: We present modal aphasia, a systematic dissociation in which current unified multimodal models accurately memorize concepts visually but fail to articulate them in writing, despite being trained on images and text simultaneously. For one, we show that leading frontier models can generate near-perfect reproductions of iconic movie artwork, but confuse crucial details when asked for textual descriptions. We corroborate those findings through controlled experiments on synthetic datasets in multiple architectures. Our experiments confirm that modal aphasia reliably emerges as a fundamental property of current unified multimodal models, not just as a training artifact. In practice, modal aphasia can introduce vulnerabilities in AI safety frameworks, as safeguards applied to one modality may leave harmful concepts accessible in other modalities. We demonstrate this risk by showing how a model aligned solely on text remains capable of generating unsafe images.
